courses.title: Scripting: PowerShell
courses.description: Learn PowerShell from the console to real automation — cmdlets, the object pipeline, scripts, and practical admin tasks.

content.intro: PowerShell is a shell and scripting language built on .NET. Commands are cmdlets in a consistent Verb-Noun form.

p: Windows PowerShell (5.1) ships with Windows; PowerShell 7+ (cross-platform) is a separate install. Run it in the console or VS Code.

sections.code:
Get-Process
Get-Service
Get-Command *service*   # discover commands
Get-Help Get-Process -Examples  # learn any command

note.text: Get-Command finds cmdlets; Get-Help explains them. You rarely need to memorize — you explore.

content.practice: Write the command to find help (with examples) for Get-Service.

quiz.p: To see usage examples for a cmdlet use…

content.intro: PowerShell's superpower: cmdlets pass .NET objects (not text) down the pipeline, so you can filter and shape data precisely.

p: Get-Process returns process objects with properties (Name, CPU, Id). Pipe them to other cmdlets to refine.

sections.code:
Get-Process | Where-Object CPU -gt 100      # filter
Get-Process | Select-Object Name, CPU        # pick columns
Get-Process | Sort-Object CPU -Descending    # order

note.text: Pipe to Get-Member to see an object's properties and methods: Get-Process | Get-Member.

content.practice: Write a pipeline that lists the top 5 processes by CPU, showing only Name and CPU.

quiz.p: The pipeline passes what between cmdlets?
Which filters objects by a condition?
To see an object's properties/methods, pipe to…

content.intro: Store and compare data with variables, arrays, and hashtables.

sections.code:
$name = 'Ada'
$count = 42
$items = @('a','b','c')       # array
$user = @{ Name='Ada'; Age=36 } # hashtable

note.text: PowerShell uses -eq, not == (== is not a PowerShell operator).

content.practice: Declare a hashtable for a server (name + IP) and access the IP.

content.intro: Make decisions and repeat work with conditionals and loops.

note.text: $_ (or $PSItem) is the current object inside Where-Object/ForEach-Object.

content.practice: Write a foreach loop that prints the name of every stopped service.

quiz.p: Inside ForEach-Object, the current item is…
Which handles multiple discrete cases cleanly?

quiz.ex: It runs the block per element.

content.intro: Package reusable logic into functions and save scripts as .ps1 files.

p: Save commands in a .ps1 file and run it. Parameters via param() at the top make scripts reusable.

note.text: Scripts may be blocked by execution policy. Set-ExecutionPolicy RemoteSigned (admin) allows local scripts; understand the security trade-off.

content.practice: Write a function with a parameter that returns free space for a given drive.

quiz.p: PowerShell script files use the extension…

content.intro: Put it together: query the system, filter, and export — the essence of admin automation.

sections.code:
# Top 5 CPU consumers to CSV
Get-Process | Sort-Object CPU -Descending |
  Select-Object -First 5 Name, CPU |
  Export-Csv top.csv -NoTypeInformation

# Stopped services
Get-Service | Where-Object Status -eq 'Stopped'

ul: Schedule scripts with Task Scheduler for recurring automation

note.text: Explore with Get-Command/Get-Member, build a one-liner, then save it as a script.

content.practice: Write a one-liner that exports all stopped services to a CSV file.

quiz.ex: Task Scheduler runs scripts on a schedule.

content.intro: Production scripts must fail safely. Handle errors, control their behavior, and debug when things break.

note.text: In the real world: Cmdlet errors are non-terminating by default — without -ErrorAction Stop your catch block never runs and a broken script keeps going.

p: Set-PSBreakpoint or the VS Code debugger; Write-Verbose with -Verbose for traceable output.

content.practice: Wrap a file read in try/catch so a missing file logs a warning instead of crashing.

quiz.p: Which makes a cmdlet error catchable by try/catch?
quiz.ex: Non-terminating errors need -ErrorAction Stop to be caught.

The most recent error is in…

content.intro: Run commands on remote machines and extend PowerShell with modules from the Gallery.

sections.code:
Get-Module -ListAvailable
Import-Module ActiveDirectory
Install-Module -Name Pester   # from PSGallery

note.text: In the real world: Admins rarely log into servers one by one — Invoke-Command runs a fix across dozens of machines at once, and modules (like ActiveDirectory) are how real admin tasks get automated.

content.practice: Write a command that runs Get-Service on a remote server named SRV01.

quiz.p: Which runs a scriptblock on a remote host?
A reusable, persistent remote connection is a…

content.intro: Combine parameters, pipeline input, and logging into a script you'd actually run in production.

note.text: In the real world: This is how routine ops actually run: a parameterized script + Task Scheduler handles nightly cleanups, user offboarding, and report generation without anyone touching a console.

quiz.p: A safe dry-run is enabled by supporting…

content.intro: Bulk file work is the bread and butter of scripting — enumerate, filter, and act on files at scale.

sections.code:
Get-ChildItem C:\logs -Recurse -Filter *.log
Get-ChildItem | Where-Object Length -gt 1MB
Get-ChildItem -Directory   # folders only

Copy-Item a.txt D:\backup\
Move-Item *.tmp C:\temp\
Remove-Item old.log
New-Item -ItemType Directory -Path C:\reports

# delete logs older than 30 days
Get-ChildItem C:\logs -Recurse -File |
  Where-Object LastWriteTime -lt (Get-Date).AddDays(-30) |
  Remove-Item -Force

note.text: In the real world: Automated log/temp cleanup on a schedule is one of the first scripts every admin writes — it reclaims disk before it becomes an outage.

content.practice: Write a pipeline that deletes .tmp files older than 7 days under C:\temp.

quiz.ex: Where-Object filters on the Length property.

content.intro: Automate the user lifecycle in Active Directory — the highest-value admin automation.

sections.code:
Import-Module ActiveDirectory
Get-ADUser -Filter "Enabled -eq 'True'" -Properties LastLogonDate
Search-ADAccount -LockedOut
Search-ADAccount -AccountInactive -TimeSpan 90.00:00:00

Set-ADUser abyte -Department 'IT'
Add-ADGroupMember 'Helpdesk' -Members abyte
Disable-ADAccount abyte

note.text: In the real world: Onboarding and offboarding are almost entirely scriptable — New-ADUser + group adds on hire, Disable-ADAccount + group removal on exit. This is a top interview talking point.

content.intro: Run scripts on a schedule and query deep system info via CIM/WMI.

sections.code:

$t = New-ScheduledTaskTrigger -Daily -At 6am

content.intro: Combine everything into a real deliverable: a scheduled system health report.

p: Build a script that gathers disk space, stopped auto-start services, and recent system errors, then writes a timestamped report and (optionally) emails it — scheduled daily.

note.text: In the real world: This single script is portfolio-worthy — it demonstrates CIM, filtering, error handling, exporting, and scheduling: exactly what a junior admin role expects.

content.intro: Talk to web services directly from the shell — the glue between tools.

sections.code:

     -Headers @{ Authorization = 'Bearer TOKEN' }
$r.servers

content.intro: Script reliable, dated, self-pruning backups.

sections.code:
$stamp = Get-Date -Format yyyyMMdd
Copy-Item C:\data\* "D:\backup\$stamp\" -Recurse -Force

Compress-Archive C:\data "D:\backup\data_$stamp.zip"
# keep 14 days
Get-ChildItem D:\backup\*.zip |
  Where-Object LastWriteTime -lt (Get-Date).AddDays(-14) |
  Remove-Item

note.text: In the real world: A backup script that dates archives and prunes old ones enforces retention automatically — pair it with an offsite copy to satisfy the 3-2-1 rule.

courses.title: Scripting: Python
courses.description: Learn Python for IT: from syntax and data structures to files, errors, and real automation scripts.

content.intro: Python is a readable, general-purpose language. Run it interactively or as .py files.

sections.code:
python --version      # check version
python script.py      # run a file
# interactive REPL:
>>> print('Hello')
Hello

name = 'Ada'
count = 42
print(f'{name} has {count} items')   # f-string

note.text: Python uses indentation (not braces) to define blocks — be consistent (4 spaces).

content.practice: Write a line that prints a name and count using an f-string.

content.intro: Python's built-in types and collections cover most needs.

sections.code:
fruits = ['apple', 'pear']      # list (ordered, mutable)
point = (3, 4)                  # tuple (immutable)
user = {'name': 'Ada', 'age': 36}  # dict (key/value)
unique = {1, 2, 3}              # set (unique)

note.text: fruits[0] → 'apple'; user['name'] → 'Ada'; len(fruits) → length.

    return shutil.disk_usage(path).free / 1e9

pip install requests

sections.code:

re.findall(r'\d+', 'a1 b2 c3')     # ['1','2','3']

m.group(1)                         # 'ada'

note.text: In the real world: Extracting IPs, timestamps, or error codes from thousands of log lines is a regex one-liner — this is the single most reused skill in IT scripting.

content.intro: CSV is the universal exchange format for IT data — read and write it cleanly.

sections.code:
import csv
with open('users.csv', newline='') as f:
    for row in csv.DictReader(f):
        print(row['email'])

with open('out.csv','w',newline='') as f:
    w = csv.DictWriter(f, fieldnames=['host','status'])
    w.writeheader()
    w.writerow({'host':'srv01','status':'up'})

note.text: In the real world: DictReader turns each row into a dict keyed by header — feed a CSV of new hires straight into an account-creation loop.

content.practice: Write a loop that prints the 'email' column of every row in users.csv.

quiz.ex: newline='' avoids blank rows on Windows.

content.intro: JSON is how APIs and config files speak — parse and produce it.

data = json.loads('{"name":"srv01"}')
data['name']
json.dumps({'ok':True}, indent=2)

    cfg = json.load(f)
with open('out.json','w') as f:
    json.dump(cfg, f, indent=2)

note.text: In the real world: Nearly every REST response is JSON — json handling is the bridge between an API call and a usable Python object.

tree = ET.parse('data.xml')
root = tree.getroot()
for item in root.findall('item'):
    print(item.get('id'), item.text)
root = ET.fromstring('1') root.find('a').text # '1'

note.text: In the real world: Windows event exports, some monitoring feeds, and older APIs return XML — ElementTree extracts the fields you need without extra dependencies.

quiz.p: An attribute value is read with…

content.intro: Real APIs need auth, handle paging, and fail — write clients that cope.

sections.code:
import requests
r = requests.get(url, headers={'Authorization':f'Bearer {token}'}, timeout=10)
r.raise_for_status()
data = r.json()

results, page = [], 1
while True:
    r = requests.get(url, params={'page':page}).json()
    results += r['items']
    if not r.get('next'): break
    page += 1

note.text: In the real world: Timeouts, raise_for_status, and retry/backoff separate a script that dies at 2am from one that logs the error and moves on — essential for unattended automation.

content.practice: Write a paginated GET loop that stops when there's no 'next' page.

quiz.p: Stop a script on HTTP errors with…

content.intro: Run commands on remote Linux hosts from Python — core cross-platform admin.

sections.code:
import paramiko
c = paramiko.SSHClient()
c.set_missing_host_key_policy(paramiko.AutoAddPolicy())
c.connect('host', username='admin', key_filename='~/.ssh/id_rsa')
stdin, stdout, stderr = c.exec_command('df -h')
print(stdout.read().decode())
c.close()

note.text: In the real world: Paramiko lets one script push a command or config to dozens of Linux servers — the Python equivalent of PowerShell remoting for the *nix side of the house.

content.practice: Write the calls to connect via key auth and run 'uptime' on a remote host.

quiz.ex: Paramiko is the standard SSH lib.

content.intro: Check reachability and ports from Python for diagnostics and monitoring.

sections.code:
import socket
def port_open(host, port, t=2):
    with socket.socket() as s:
        s.settimeout(t)
        return s.connect_ex((host, port)) == 0
port_open('srv01', 443)

import subprocess
subprocess.run(['ping','-c','1','host'], capture_output=True)

note.text: In the real world: A short socket loop can scan a list of hosts/ports to confirm a service rollout — faster and more repeatable than manual telnet checks.

content.practice: Write a function that returns True if a TCP port is open on a host.

content.intro: Read live system metrics in Python and alert on thresholds.

sections.code:
import psutil
psutil.cpu_percent(interval=1)
psutil.virtual_memory().percent
psutil.disk_usage('/').percent

if psutil.disk_usage('/').percent > 90:
    print('ALERT: disk over 90%')

note.text: In the real world: psutil works on Windows and Linux, so one monitoring script covers a mixed fleet — schedule it and pipe alerts to email or a webhook.

content.practice: Write a check that alerts when memory usage exceeds 85%.

content.intro: Send reports and alerts programmatically with smtplib.

sections.code:
import smtplib
from email.message import EmailMessage
m = EmailMessage()
m['From']='bot@corp'; m['To']='it@corp'; m['Subject']='Disk alert'
m.set_content('srv01 disk at 92%')
with smtplib.SMTP('smtp.corp', 587) as s:
    s.starttls(); s.login('bot','pw'); s.send_message(m)

p: Use m.add_attachment(...) to attach a CSV/HTML report generated by your script.

note.text: In the real world: Wiring monitoring + email means the system tells you about problems — the shift from reactive ('users reported it') to proactive ('the script caught it first').

content.practice: Outline the steps to send an alert email with a CSV attachment.

content.intro: Batch file operations with os, shutil, and pathlib.

sections.code:
import shutil, os
shutil.copy('a.txt','backup/')
shutil.move('b.tmp','archive/')
os.remove('old.log')

for i, p in enumerate(Path('.').glob('*.jpg')):
    p.rename(f'img_{i:03}.jpg')

p: Read a list of hosts, check each host's reachability and (via SSH) disk usage, and produce a report of hosts over 85% disk.

sections.code:
import paramiko, csv
results = []
for host in open('hosts.txt').read().split():
    try:
        c = paramiko.SSHClient(); c.set_missing_host_key_policy(paramiko.AutoAddPolicy())
        c.connect(host, username='admin', timeout=5)
        out = c.exec_command('df -h / | tail -1')[1].read().decode()
        results.append({'host':host, 'disk':out.split()[4]})
        c.close()
    except Exception as e:
        results.append({'host':host, 'disk':f'ERR {e}'})

p: Every run: gather CPU, memory, and disk via psutil; if any exceeds its threshold, send an email alert; always append a timestamped row to a CSV history.

import psutil, csv, smtplib
from datetime import datetime
from email.message import EmailMessage

m = {'time':datetime.now().isoformat(),
     'cpu':psutil.cpu_percent(1),
     'mem':psutil.virtual_memory().percent,
     'disk':psutil.disk_usage('/').percent}
with open('health.csv','a',newline='') as f:
    csv.DictWriter(f, fieldnames=m).writerow(m)
